sec.title: Background
sec.p: Accurate prediction of pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant chemotherapy has significant clinical utility in the management of breast cancer treatment. Although multimodal deep learning models have shown promise for predicting pCR from medical imaging and other clinical data, their adoption has been limited due to challenges with interpretability and generalizability across institutions.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We developed a multimodal deep learning model combining post contrast-enhanced whole-breast MRI at pre- and post-treatment timepoints with non-imaging clinical features. The model integrates 3D convolutional neural networks and self-attention to capture spatial and cross-modal interactions. We utilized two public multi-institutional datasets to perform internal and external validation of the model. For model training and validation, we used data from the I-SPY 2 trial (N = 660). For external validation, we used the I-SPY 1 dataset (N = 114).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of the 660 patients in I-SPY 2, 217 patients achieved pCR (32.88%). Of the 114 patients in I-SPY 1, 29 achieved pCR (25.44%). The attention-based multimodal model yielded the best predictive performance with an AUC of 0.73 ± 0.04 on the internal data and an AUC of 0.71 ± 0.02 on the external dataset. The MRI-only model (internal AUC = 0.68 ± 0.03, external AUC = 0.70 ± 0.04) and the non-MRI clinical features-only model (internal AUC = 0.66 ± 0.08, external AUC = 0.71 ± 0.03) trailed in performance, indicating the combination of both modalities is most effective.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We present a robust and interpretable deep learning framework for pCR prediction in breast cancer patients undergoing NAC. By combining imaging and clinical data with attention-based fusion, the model achieves strong predictive performance and generalizes across institutions.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is widely employed in the treatment of breast cancer. Its primary goals are to reduce tumor burden in locally advanced cases in order to permit more conservative surgery, and to assess tumor response in aggressive subtypes to guide and personalize subsequent treatment [1]. Pathological complete response (pCR), defined as the absence of invasive cancer after NAC, is a key prognostic indicator often linked to improved progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival [2, 3]. Despite its clinical importance, early prediction of pCR remains elusive. Radiological assessments of NAC response offer a non-invasive and promising alternative to traditional biopsy-based pathological assessments. Developing reliable methods to predict NAC efficacy early in the treatment course could help to guide clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes.

Studies have successfully applied machine learning (ML) models to breast MRI data to predict pCR. Originally, most ML studies involved traditional methods such as support vector machines, random forests, and decision trees, among others. These methods can be work and time intensive as they often use manually extracted image features, such as tumor volume, diameter, or radiomic characteristics, relying on radiologists to contour tumors and identify relevant features for training [4, 5].

In recent years, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful tool in medical imaging analysis. Studies have shown that AI systems can detect breast cancer from MRI with similar or better accuracy than experienced radiologists [6]. To this end, deep learning models have been used to detect and segment breast tumors from MRI [7]. For example, U-Net-based architectures have been widely adopted for segmentation in breast MRI, achieving high accuracy and reproducibility in delineating tumor boundaries [8, 9]. Using these segmentation models facilitates precise quantification of tumor size and morphology.

More recent studies have explored the application of DL models on whole-breast MRI data without manual contouring or tumor annotations. In addition, newer studies have adopted multimodal models, which utilize more than one modality for their prediction [10, 11]. Multimodal models integrating MRI data with clinical information have demonstrated promise in providing more robust predictions. We compared our attention-based multimodal deep learning model with several ML models and demonstrated that the deep learning model outperformed traditional ML methods. The methodology we implemented regarding preprocessing, model architecture, training procedures, and evaluation metrics are explained in detail.

There are key challenges that impede widespread use of these technologies in clinical practice, which we have attempted to address. A major challenge is the generalizability of models across institutions. Medical imaging protocols, data quality, and patient profiles vary significantly between centers, leading to reduced performance when models trained on one institution’s dataset are applied to another institution’s dataset. This was the basis for incorporating two large multi-center datasets (I-SPY 2 for training and internal validation and I-SPY 1 for external validation) in our study, which provides validation of our model’s performance across multiple institutions and a diverse array of protocols. Another critical challenge is the so-called “black box” problem, where the high complexity of deep learning models hinders interpretability, making it difficult to understand the rationale behind their predictions and hindering the broader clinical adoption of this technology [12–14]. Grad-CAM heatmaps included in our study provide visual confirmation of the model’s ability to reliably identify tumors. Attention weights incorporated in our study design show the relative importance assigned by the model, providing some rationale to its predictions.

In this study, we present a multimodal deep learning model with four key contributions to predict breast cancer pCR. First, we used a multi-head self-attention mechanism to combine MRI data from two time points with non-imaging clinical data (such as demographics and molecular subtypes) into our deep learning model. Second, we trained and tested two multi-center datasets to improve generalizability of our model. Third, the model operates on whole-breast 3D MRI without manual cropping of the breast or tumor segmentation, which eliminates a potential source of bias and increases efficiency. Lastly, we enhanced the model’s interpretability by incorporating attention outputs, generating heatmaps, and evaluating contribution of individual clinical features, offering insights into the model’s decision-making process and providing clinicians with a more transparent understanding of how predictions are made.

sec.title: Data sources
I-SPY 2 trial dataset
I-SPY 1 trial dataset
sec.p: I-SPY 1 (Investigation of Serial studies to Predict Your Therapeutic Response with Imaging and moLecular analysis 1/ACRIN 6657) was a prospective multi-center trial designed to evaluate MRI for ability to predict response to treatment and risk-of-recurrence in patients also with stage II or III cancer receiving NAC. This trial, conducted between 2002 and 2006, enrolled 237 patients, of which 230 met the eligibility criteria (Fig. 1B). Patients underwent anthracycline-cyclophosphamide chemotherapy with or without taxane, and MRI data was collected before, during, and after treatment. The primary endpoints were pCR and recurrence-free survival (RFS). Non-MRI data for each patient included age, race, estrogen receptor status (ER), progesterone receptor status (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status, 3-level hormonal receptor (HR)/HER2 category, bilateral breast cancer category, and tumor laterality. For our external validation, the Level 3 curated dataset was used, which consisted of 162 patients. Of these 162 subjects, a further 46 were excluded, leaving a testing set of 114 patients. Only the clinical features that were available in the ISPY2 dataset used during training were included (HR status, HER2 status, age, race) and menopausal status was set to N/A since it was not available.

sec.title: Preprocessing
sec.p: The first post-contrast MRI taken at pre-treatment (T1) and post-treatment (T4) were extracted from the unilateral cropped DCE-MRI for both datasets. The MRI exams were downloaded as DICOM images after which they were loaded and preprocessed using the PyDicom (V2.4.4), SimpleITK (V2.3.1), NumPy (V1.25.2), and Torchio (V0.19.7) libraries [18–21]. All images were normalized and cropped to a 3D NumPy array with a fixed dimension of 80 by 256 by 256. For images with more than 80 slices, the middle 80 slices were extracted. For images with fewer than 80 slices, zero-pad slices were added at each end of the image. During training, further augmentation of random flipping along the height and width dimensions was performed for generalization.

sec.title: System architecture
sec.p:
The model input consisted of a multimodal data combining first post-contrast 3D dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) volumes from two treatment timepoints, pre-treatment (T1) and post-treatment (T4), along with clinical data (Fig. 2). Each patient’s clinical features included hormone receptor (HR) status, HER2 status, age, race, and menopausal status.Fig. 2
Overall architecture of the model. A The model employs a 3D resnet-50 as the backbone image encoder. Clinical features of HR, HER2, age, race, and menopausal status are collected, normalized, and converted before being fed through FCL (fully connected layers). B The stack of encoded latent vectors is fed to a transformer block consisting of multi-headed self-attention, feed forward layers, and residual connections

The selection of T1 and T4 MRIs was based on their clinical relevance: T1 provides a baseline assessment of the tumor prior to treatment, while T4, as the post-treatment MRI, captures the cumulative effects of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), reflecting the most significant changes indicative of treatment response. This approach aligns with existing studies, such as Dammu et al.’s work on the I-SPY 1 dataset, which demonstrated the efficacy of combining T1 and T4 in capturing the progression of NAC treatment [10].

The architecture integrated a 3D convolutional neural network (3D ResNet) for MRI feature extraction and fully connected layers to encode the clinical data [22]. Clinical features were encoded via fully connected layers to produce a feature vector matching the dimension of the MRI encodings. The extracted latent representations from both MRI time points and clinical data were then fused in a transformer block, which employed multi-head self-attention to weigh the relevance of each modality and prioritize cross-modality information.

sec.title: Cross validation, training, and performance metrics
sec.p:
We used five-fold cross-validation on the I-SPY2 dataset, splitting it into 528 training samples and 132 validation samples per fold. To assess the model’s generalizability, we also performed external validation using the I-SPY 1 dataset (n = 114) (Fig. 3). Predictive performance was systematically assessed using the following objective metrics: receiver operative character curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. For comparison, we trained and tested with three other model architectures: a model taking in only the MRI, a model taking in only the clinical features, and a multimodal model using concatenation instead of attention.Fig. 3
Training and evaluation flowchart

During training, dropout with a probability of 0.1 was included in the fully connected layers and feed forward networks to address overfitting [26]. Several optimizers were tested, but the Adam optimizer was ultimately used. A batch size of 4 was used with a learning rate of 0.001, and early stopping of the training was performed to prevent overfitting.

sec.title: Visualization methods
sec.p: To interpret the logic behind our model’s predictions, we apply two visualization techniques: Grad-CAM and attention weights from multi-head self-attention.

Grad-CAM is a well-established visualization method commonly used with CNN-based models to highlight the areas of an image that contribute most to a specific prediction. It works by computing the gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer of the network, which are then used to determine the importance of each spatial location in the feature map. This allows us to generate a heatmap that emphasizes the regions of the input image most relevant to the model’s decision.

The resulting Grad-CAM heatmap assigns higher values to regions that strongly influence the model’s prediction, with brighter or warmer colors (e.g., red, yellow) indicating higher relevance. Conversely, cooler colors (e.g., blue) represent areas with minimal contribution. In our case, the heatmaps consistently highlight tumor regions as the most significant contributors, confirming that the model primarily focuses on these areas when making its classification. As shown in Fig. 4, our model focused on the tumor and peri-tumor regions to make the prediction of pCR, which provides valuable insight into the areas that most influence the model’s decision and supports the clinical relevance of these regions in an interpretable way.Fig. 4
Grad-CAM showing the regions of the input MRI that were most pivotal in the model’s pCR prediction. Areas with the red-most regions impact the model’s final decision the most

Our model’s multi-head attention mechanism operates by assigning weights to different parts of the input data to determine their relative importance in making predictions. We represent these values in a 3 × 3 table, where each row corresponds to a query modality and each column to a key modality. Diagonal values represent self-attention, highlighting the degree to which each modality relies on its own features, while the off-diagonal values capture cross-modal interactions. For example, the weight in the first row and third column indicates how much the T1 MRI attends to the clinical features, and the weight in the second row and second column indicates how much T4 MRI paid attention to itself.

Figure 5A shows an example of an attention weight table for a patient on the left. Of the three diagonal values for T1 MRI, T4 MRI, and clinical features, we have the highest attention value of 0.64 on the clinical features, whereas the values for the MRIs are lower at 0.3 and 0.31. This indicates that in this patient’s case, the clinical features rely more heavily on their own information when contributing to the prediction compared to the MRIs. On the non-diagonal entries, the attention that the clinical features pay to the MRIs are relatively low at 0.18 for both, whereas the attention the two MRIs pay to the clinical features are higher at 0.38 and 0.39. This shows that clinical features rely less on the input from imaging data than the images do on the clinical features. The clinical features demonstrate the strongest self-attention, suggesting they are critical and provide independent, non-redundant information for predicting pCR. This contrasts with the MRI modalities (T1 and T4), which have balanced attention weights across self-attention and cross-modal attention. Finally, the values on the table can be summed by column to obtain a total “importance” score for that modality (Fig. 5B). This can be used to conclude which of the input modalities the model is most affected by in making its final pCR prediction.Fig. 5
Attention weight table for a sample patient prediction. A Attention weights show the amount of importance the model assigned in making its prediction. The 3 × 3 heat map shows how much each modality pays attention to the other inputs. B The values can be summed by each column and normalized to obtain a value of importance of each modality, represented in the bar chart. In this patient’s case, clinical features have the highest contribution followed by similar contributions by the two MRIs

The aggregated results over the validation dataset (Supplementary Fig. 1) show that the two MRI have a slightly greater impact on the final prediction compared to the clinical features, highlighting the importance of radiological data for pCR prediction. The attention weights between the two MRIs are also higher, suggesting that the model emphasizes the distinct temporal differences between the pre- and post-treatment MRI scans.

In addition, we performed a feature perturbation analysis (Supplemental Fig. 2) on the validation set to assess each feature’s impact on prediction performance. For each feature, we randomly shuffled its values across patients and measured the resulting drop in AUC and accuracy. HER2 status produced the most significant decrease in performance, followed by HR status. The remaining features (age, race, and menopausal status) showed minimal to no change. Similar patterns were observed across both metrics. These findings are consistent with previous reports in the literature [10].

sec.title: Comparison against traditional ML methods
Results
sec.p:
The I-SPY 2 dataset is a more challenging dataset than the I-SPY 1 dataset. While both datasets are multi-institutional, the I-SPY1 dataset’s MRI seem to have more consistent and uniform imaging. In addition, the I-SPY 2 MRIs are axial, whereas I-SPY 1 MRIs are sagittal (Fig. 7).Fig. 7
Sample first-post contrast unilateral DCE-MRI from (A) the I-SPY 1 and (B) I-SPY 2 dataset. I-SPY 1 images are sagittal and I-SPY 2 images are axial. Both are middle slices from 3D volumes with normalization and cropping applied

sec.title: Performance compared to traditional ML methods
Discussion
sec.p: We showed that an attention-based deep learning model can learn to combine multiple treatment time points of 3D post-contrast MRIs and other clinical data to predict pathological complete response (pCR) in breast cancer patients. Our model used a fusion multimodal deep learning approach that takes in the whole-breast MRI without any manual cropping of the breast or the tumor regions. Using a large multi-institutional dataset of 660 patients (I-SPY 2) for training and internal validation, our model achieved an AUC of 0.73. Using another institutional dataset (I-SPY 1) for external validation yielded an AUC of 0.71. Our deep learning model outperformed all four traditional ML methods in both AUC and accuracy, as well as a more balanced sensitivity and specificity.

Several studies have applied different deep learning methods to pCR prediction. Khan et al. [12] conducted a systematic review of deep learning pCR prediction models, ultimately analyzing 13 studies, and highlighted common challenges with generalizability. Our study addresses this limitation by utilizing both internal and external validation, improving the robustness of our findings. For example, the model by Joo et al. [11] was trained and tested on a single-institutional dataset. Dammu et al. [10] incorporated multi-time point MRI from the I-SPY 1 dataset to predict pCR, achieving an AUC of 0.83 with pre-treatment (T1) and post-treatment (T4) MRIs. However, their model relied on a smaller sample size. By contrast, our study leveraged the larger I-SPY 2 dataset and demonstrated consistent performance across both internal and external datasets. These prior studies did not provide interpretation methods.

One challenge in this study stemmed from the differences in imaging planes between the datasets. While both I-SPY 1 and I-SPY 2 consisted of unilateral breast MRIs, the former captures sagittal views, whereas the latter used axial views. This difference in anatomical perspectives is one example of how breast cancer MRI protocols could vary across institutions, complicating the generalization of imaging models. In our data augmentation techniques, we used translation, rotation, and flipping, which were designed to promote invariance to such variations. Future work could explore further training strategies or model architectural modifications that explicitly account for imaging plane variations, such as spatial transformer networks. Vision transformers (ViT) could also be a viable alternative.

In addition to generalizability, this study also addressed the “black box” nature of the deep learning approach which is a frequently cited challenge for clinical adoption. We provided both qualitative and quantitative interpretation methods using Grad-CAM and attention value tables. The Grad-CAM heatmaps highlight regions within the MRI that contributed most significantly to the model’s final predictions. Observing tumor regions with high activation provided a visual sanity check, reassuring users that the model focuses on relevant anatomical structures.

The attention weight table provided valuable insights into the model’s reasoning by illustrating the interactions between imaging timepoints and clinical features. For instance, strong attention from T1 MRI to T4 MRI highlighted the importance of tracking tumor progression over time for accurate pCR predictions. Similarly, if clinical features showed strong attention to T4 MRI, it would mean that the model utilized later imaging data to contextualize clinical information. These patterns helped determine whether different modalities contributed independently or work synergistically in making predictions. High self-attention values indicated unique contribution from a specific modality, whereas high cross-modal attention value indicated complementary relationships, such as clinical features enhancing the interpretation of imaging data. To quantify each modality’s contributions, attention weights can be summed and normalized across columns, providing a clear metric of their relative impact on the final prediction. By combining visualization tools, clinicians and researchers can better understand the logic behind the model’s predictions, identify potential issues with imaging data quality or modality-specific limitations, and guide improvements in data collection, preprocessing, and model development.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Our study has several limitations. First, while our model demonstrates promise in predicting pCR, there is room for improvement in its predictive performance. The I-SPY 2 images exhibit a wider range of MRI quality, with variations in image acquisition protocols and noise levels. Additionally, the unilateral cropping of bilateral MRIs results in variability in breast-to-non-breast region ratios, potentially introducing confusion for the model. To address this inconsistency, future work could use segmentation methods to isolate the tumor or breast regions. By using segmentation models to delineate regions of interest, the model could focus attention on more clinically relevant features and reduce noise from surrounding non-tumor tissue. Integrating segmentation-guided features as an additional input could enhance the predictive performance and interpretability.

Class imbalance was another challenge (pCR was 33%). To address this, we used a combination of binary cross-entropy and focal loss to emphasize harder-to-classify cases. While this strategy helped balance sensitivity and specificity to an extent, sensitivity was still consistently lower than specificity across models. Future work could explore additional methods such as class-weighted loss functions or sampling techniques to further mitigate imbalance effects, though we believe that expanding to larger and more diverse datasets will be essential for improving minority class performance.

Our study only used the first post-contrast T1-weighted images. Incorporating additional imaging modalities, such as T1-weighted subtracted images, T2-weighted images, and diffusion-weighted imaging, could provide richer feature sets for the model to learn from.

While our external testing on the I-SPY 1 dataset strengthens the robustness of our results, this study was constrained to unilateral images, as I-SPY 1 does not include bilateral images. Furthermore, while this study focuses on pCR prediction, the potential exists to predict other clinically significant endpoints, such as residual cancer burden, progression-free survival, recurrence risk, and overall survival, which remain underexplored. These limitations underscore the broader challenge of limited access to large, diverse public datasets, which remains a barrier to achieving generalizability and broader clinical adoption of DL methods in pCR prediction.
NAC regimens of the I-SPY2 dataset were not modeled because of the small sample sizes within each treatment group.

Finally, our model is subject to challenges inherent to all DL methods, including potential overfitting due to limited sample sizes relative to model complexity. Although visualization techniques such as Grad-CAM and attention maps were employed in our study to improve interpretability, further work is needed to establish intuitive and clinically relevant evaluation metrics that align with physician needs and patient outcomes, beyond standard technical measures of AUC and accuracy.

Addressing these challenges will require ongoing innovation in model design, larger and more diverse datasets, and rigorous clinical validation to improve the reliability, generalizability, and interpretability of DL models for pCR prediction. By demonstrating external validation and employing visualization techniques, our study takes steps toward addressing some of these broader challenges, but further research is necessary to fully realize the potential of DL in this domain.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we developed and applied an attention-based fusion approach to multimodal deep learning prediction of pCR in breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy from two multi-institutional datasets. We showed a method for combining MRI and other clinical data into a model’s inference with competitive, interpretable, and generalizable results.
